boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Stettin entry (capitulation, 29 October 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: General Lasalle's light cavalry, with Belliard sent by Murat, before the fortress of Stettin held by General Romberg's garrison, from the French arrival at midday on the 29th to the garrison's laying down of arms at daybreak on the 30th. The prisoners' unrest after the surrender and the occupation of the place by Lannes's corps are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Prussian) as the fortress garrison of 5,300 Prussians (among them 100 officers) with 281 guns under Major General v. Romberg, which capitulated without a stroke of the sword before 800 French hussars under Brigadier General Count Lasalle (side A, French). By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison as 100 officers and 5184 men and its guns as 187 serviceable and 94 usable in an emergency, which total 5284 men and 281 guns (our arithmetic); the French letters give other figures (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french, side-a-strength). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 29/10. capitulation of Stettin'; 'before 800 French hussars under Brigadier General Count Lasalle the fortress occupied by 5,300 Prussians (among them 100 officers) with 281 guns under Major General v. Romberg capitulates without a stroke of the sword. The officers were released on their word of honour; the men went into captivity'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: the garrison consisted of the 3rd musketeer battalions of the regiments Kunheim, Arnim, Möllendorf, Larisch, Winning, Braunschweig-Oels and Pirch and a fortress artillery company, or 100 officers and 5184 men, whose good will made the bravest resistance possible. It could have been much increased by taking in the officers, NCOs and men passing through in large numbers and arming them with the muskets sent from Berlin to Stettin in two barges, and its total want of cavalry could have been remedied; but the governor kept back no man for fortress duty. The fortress had 187 fully serviceable guns and 94 still usable in an emergency, of which 100 of various calibres were already mounted on the ramparts and the most important points of defence when the French arrived.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page image of p. 217. The garrison and guns were the place's own before the French arrived, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's officers and men total 5284 and his guns 281 (our arithmetic). English renderings (ours): 'the garrison consisted of the 3rd musketeer battalions of the regiments Kunheim, Arnim, Möllendorf, Larisch, Winning, Braunschweig-Oels and Pirch and a fortress artillery company, or of 100 officers 5184 men, whose good will made the bravest resistance possible'; 'this garrison could have been very considerably increased if the officers, NCOs and privates passing through in great numbers had been taken in and armed with the muskets sent from Berlin to Stettin in two barges; likewise the total lack of cavalry could have been fully remedied'; 'but the governor saw fit not only to keep back no man for fortress duty, but he even refused General Bila II passage and thereby caused the capitulation of Anklam, as will be shown later'; 'in guns the fortress had 187 fully serviceable pieces and 94 still usable in an emergency, of which, at the time of the French arrival, 100 pieces of various calibres were already set up on the ramparts and the most important points of defence'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: Lasalle wrote to Murat on the evening of 30 October that 5,500 men and 120 pieces of ordnance had been taken at Stettin. The 24th Bulletin, of 31 October, gave the place 160 guns and a garrison of 6,000 men of fine troops, taken prisoner, with many generals.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images; not reconciled with Höpfner's or Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). Lasalle's figure is a count of the men taken, written after the garrison had marched out; the Bulletin's is a public statement. Lannes's letter of 1 November also gives figures for the garrison and for the guns found, seen only in the OCR and not restated. The garrison was the place's own, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Lasalle, 'General Lasalle to the Grand Duke of Berg. Falkenwald, 30 October 1806, 7 o'clock in the evening'; '5,500 men were taken at Stettin and 120 pieces of ordnance. General Victor having taken over the command, I no longer followed these details'; the Bulletin, '24th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Stettin is a place in good condition, well armed and well palisaded, 160 guns, considerable magazines, a garrison of 6,000 men of fine troops, prisoner, many generals; such is the result of the capitulation of Stettin, which can only be explained by the extreme discouragement that the disappearance of the great Prussian army has produced on the Oder and in all the lands of the right bank'.

claims.value: Side A (French) before Stettin: Höpfner has General Lasalle, finding the pass of Löcknitz cleared by the Prussian troops, advance on the 29th towards Stettin as far as Neuenkirchen, while the Grand Duke of Berg moved with Grouchy's dragoon division and Suchet's infantry division of Lannes's corps to Löcknitz and pushed the dragoons on to Bismark. On the alarm only a few troops of cavalry were seen from the fortress. The garrison laid down its arms before 800 enemy cavalry and 2 guns; Bodart has 800 French hussars. Murat wrote to the Emperor that the Emperor's hussars would take possession of the gates of the place at 6 that morning; Lasalle, that General Victor's infantry arrived when the Stettin prisoners threatened their officers, and that the elite battalion made those who had taken up their arms again surrender. No passage read gives a headcount for Lasalle's brigade.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, Bodart and the French letters, all read from the page images. Höpfner's 800 cavalry and 2 guns are the troops before which the garrison laid down its arms after the capitulation; Bodart's 800 hussars are the same figure. The second parlementaire's 30 to 40,000 men were a claim made to the governor (claim side-a-command), not a count. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'General Lasalle, who found the pass of Löcknitz cleared by the Prussian troops, advanced on the 29th towards Stettin as far as Neuenkirchen'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg moved with the dragoon division Grouchy and the infantry division Suchet of Lannes's corps to Löcknitz, from where the dragoons were pushed on as far as Bismark'; 'at midday on the 29th a cannon shot announced his arrival. The alarm was beaten; the garrison moved to its posts. But only'; 'a few troops of cavalry were discovered'; 'the capitulation was carried out. The garrison had to unscrew the flints from the muskets and form on the parade ground, was led out at daybreak by General Knobelsdorf to the Berlin gate, which, like the Uckermünde gate, was occupied by French cavalry, and had to lay down its arms before 800 men of enemy cavalry and 2 guns'; Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Löcknitz, 30 October 1806, 2 o'clock in the morning'; 'Lasalle was at the gates of Stettin and summoning the governor to surrender; I have the honour to send Your Majesty the capitulation. Your Majesty's hussars will take possession of the gates of the place this morning at 6 o'clock'; Lasalle, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading; 'the prisoners of Stettin wanted to revolt; they threatened and struck their officers; it was time that General Victor's infantry arrived'; 'I reopen my letter, my lord, to tell you that after I left Stettin, the garrison that had been left on the glacis tried to take up its arms again; 500 had already taken them up again; the générale was beaten, and the elite battalion made them surrender again without firing a shot'.

claims.value: The capitulation records that Lasalle summoned Fort Preussen and the town of Stettin in the name of the Grand Duke of Berg and repeated the summons with insistence after a first refusal. Höpfner: a hussar officer with a trumpeter rode at a trot to the governor, unescorted and without a blindfold, summoned him in the Grand Duke's name and urged that all resistance was vain, since the fortress was surrounded by 100,000 men and Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau; at 4 in the afternoon a second parlementaire declared that Lasalle stood with the advance guard ½ mile from the town, that the corps of Murat and Lannes would take the fortress the next morning with 30 to 40,000 men, and that if the governor did not surrender within 12 hours the town would have to pay ½ million Thaler besides the contribution to be demanded of it. The parlementaire accepted the governor's draft except the free withdrawal, and in the night brought it back translated into French with that condition changed to the garrison's disadvantage. Belliard, sent by Murat to Stettin to summon the commandant, found that Lasalle had begun the work and let him finish it, having the replies to the governor's demands put in; he approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order. Lasalle came into the town with cavalry at 6 in the morning to sign it.
claims.rationale: The capitulation's preamble, Belliard's letter and his approval, and Höpfner's account, all read from the page images. The parlementaires' figures are their claims, not counts. English renderings (ours): the capitulation, 'after the so-called fort Preussen and the place of Stettin had been summoned by General Lasalle in the name of His Imperial and Royal Highness the Grand Duke of Berg, and this summons, after a first refusal, had been repeated with insistence, it was agreed by Lieutenant General Baron de Romberg, governor, and Major General Knobelsdorf, assisted by the engineer generals du Raudem and the engineer major de Barum, to surrender the town of Stettin and the fort of Preussen, only under the following conditions, to General Lasalle, commanding the advance guard of His Imperial and Royal Highness the Grand Duke of Berg'; Höpfner, 'immediately afterwards an enemy hussar officer appeared with a trumpeter, who, as the guards were without any instructions, rode at a trot to the governor without escort from the Prussian side and with his eyes unbandaged, and summoned him in the name of the Grand Duke of Berg to surrender'; 'he put it to the governor that all resistance was in vain, as the fortress was surrounded by 100,000 men and Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau'; 'they had not yet finished the fair copy when at 4 o'clock in the afternoon a second parlementaire appeared, who declared: General Lasalle stood with the advance guard ½ mile from the town; the corps of Prince Murat and Marshal Lannes would take the fortress the next morning with 30 to 40,000 men, and if the governor did not consent to surrender within 12 hours, the town of Stettin should be obliged to pay ½ million Thaler besides the contribution to be demanded of it'; 'after the parlementaire's return the governor therefore declared that he would surrender the fortress under the conditions already drafted. The parlementaire accepted them, but with the exception of the condition of free withdrawal, so the draft was signed by the governor and both commandants and handed to the parlementaire, who went back with it to General Lasalle'; 'in the night to the 30th the parlementaire returned to Stettin and brought back the draft translated into French, with the condition altered to the garrison's disadvantage, by which it was granted the fate of Hohenlohe's corps'; 'General Lasalle had already come into the town with cavalry in the morning at 6 o'clock to sign the capitulation, so that enemy troops were thus already in the fortress before the capitulation was signed'; Belliard, 'General Belliard to the major général. 30 October 1806'; 'I had been sent by the Prince to Stettin to summon the commandant, but Lasalle had begun the job and I let him finish it, having the replies put to the governor's demands'; 'by order of His Highness the Grand Duke of Berg and Cleves, lieutenant of the Emperor, the present capitulation seen and approved, to be carried out. The divisional general, chief of the general staff, Belliard. At Möhringen, 29 October 1806, at half past eleven in the evening'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the governor was the 81-year-old General-Lieutenant Romberg and the commandant Major General Knobelsdorf, and General Rauch, director of the engineering academy and in charge of the works, was named vice-commandant by the King. The governor kept back no man of the troops passing through for fortress duty and refused General Bila II passage, which by Höpfner's account caused the capitulation of Anklam. Romberg answered the first summons with apparent calm that he knew his duty and would defend the fortress entrusted to him to the utmost, but as soon as the parlementaire had gone he dictated to the judge-advocate Dragaud a draft capitulation: the fortress to be handed over the next morning, the garrison to have free withdrawal and march off with all marks of honour; the commandant and vice-commandant joined in, the latter dictating the end of the draft. At the second parlementaire the governor lost all composure; everyone talked at once in the Frenchman's presence and no one thought of calling the prescribed council of war; the minister Ingersleben, who had come in uninvited, took the parlementaire to his residence so that they could deliberate, and those present unanimously resolved to surrender. The governor and both commandants signed the draft. When the garrison, knowing nothing of the negotiation, fired on enemy horsemen riding too boldly forward, the governor forbade the firing. Romberg was sentenced to death by court martial in 1809 but pardoned by the King. Belliard called him an old wreck of a governor who greeted the French with a few cannon shots and surrendered at discretion after making many difficulties.
claims.rationale: Side B's conduct from Höpfner, read from the page images of pp. 216-219, and Belliard's letter from the page image of p. 527. Höpfner does not name his sources for Stettin. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the governor was the 81-year-old General-Lieutenant Romberg, the commandant Major General Knobelsdorf, the place's engineer Major Harenberg'; 'to the government 4 more engineer officers were assigned for duty; to General Rauch, director of the engineering academy, the supervision of the works was entrusted; this general was also named vice-commandant by the King'; as in claim side-b-strength for the men kept back and General Bila; 'the governor answered with apparent calm: he knew his duty and would defend the fortress entrusted to him to the utmost. So the parlementaire was dispatched at 1 o'clock midday with a refusal'; 'unfortunately these heroic sentiments of the governor were of very short duration; for hardly had the parlementaire gone when he dictated to the government's judge-advocate Dragaud a draft capitulation whose substance was: that the fortress should be handed over the next morning, and the garrison receive free withdrawal and march off with all marks of honour'; 'while they were still in full work, the commandant and vice-commandant also appeared, and the latter was charged with dictating the end of the draft, which was readily done'; 'the governor had lost all composure; he did not know what to answer the parlementaire and told him to be patient'; 'during this conversation the two commandants and several other officers of the garrison had come in; everyone talked at once in the presence of the Frenchman, and no-'; '-body thought of calling the prescribed council of war'; 'at last the minister Ingersleben, who had come in uninvited, took the parlementaire to his residence so that they could deliberate. claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Stettin on 29 October without a stroke of the sword: the officers were released on their word of honour and the men went into captivity. The capitulation, dated at Stettin on 29 October 1806 at 6 in the evening and signed by Romberg as governor, surrendered the town and Fort Preussen to Lasalle. To the garrison's request for free exit with arms and baggage it answered that the garrison would march out with the honours of war, lay down its arms on the glacis and be prisoners of war sent to France, the officers prisoners on parole with passports to go where they wished, keeping their swords, baggage, horses and all that belonged to them; everything in the place belonging to the King of Prussia was to be handed over, the Prussian troops had until noon to settle their affairs, and the Berlin gate and a post on the Oder bridge were to be occupied by the French at 6 in the morning. Below the date the print sets the words 'seen and approved the present capitulation to be carried out' above Romberg's name, followed by Lasalle's, as brigadier general, at the headquarters of Möhringen on 29 October; whose approval the words record is not shown. Belliard approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order at half past eleven that evening. Belliard wrote that the commandant capitulated at 1 in the morning. Höpfner: the capitulation was carried out; at daybreak General Knobelsdorf led the garrison out by the Berlin gate, held like the Uckermünde gate by French cavalry, and it laid down its arms before 800 enemy cavalry and 2 guns. Lasalle reported that after he left, the garrison left on the glacis tried to take up its arms again, 500 having done so, until the elite battalion made them surrender again without firing a shot.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome; the capitulation, Belliard's, Murat's and Lasalle's letters and Höpfner's account read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. The hours disagree and are kept as given: the capitulation is dated 6 in the evening of the 29th and Belliard approved it at half past eleven that night; Belliard reported that the commandant capitulated at 1 in the morning; Höpfner has the parlementaire bring back the French text in the night to the 30th and Lasalle enter the town at 6 in the morning before it was signed (claim side-a-command); Murat's covering letter is dated 2 in the morning, but Höpfner has him report at 5 in the morning. Articles 11 and 12, printed without replies, hand over the treasure in the place and name artillery and engineer officers to hand over and receive the magazines, munitions, maps and plans. Lannes wrote on 31 October that after the capitulation a rumour that the Russians were coming had made part of the garrison take up arms again, and that all was back in order (OCR). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; the capitulation, as in claim side-a-command for the preamble; 'art. 1. The whole present garrison, including the small staff and all soldiers not belonging to the garrison, shall obtain free exit with arms and baggage to go either to West and North Prussia or to Silesia'; 'reply. The garrison will march out with the honours of war, lay down its arms on the glacis, be prisoner of war and sent to France. The officers will be prisoners on parole and passports will be issued to them to go wherever they please'; 'reply. The officers will keep their swords, their baggage, their horses and all that may belong to them'; 'reply. Everything in the place belonging to His Majesty the King of Prussia will be handed over to the French troops'; 'reply. The Prussian troops will be granted until noon to arrange their affairs'; 'reply. The Berlin gate will be handed over to the French troops, who will have a post on the Oder bridge. These two posts will be occupied at 6 o'clock in the morning by the French troops'; 'art. 11. The treasure in the place will be handed over to the French troops'; 'art. 12. Artillery and engineer officers will be named on both sides to hand over and receive all the magazines, munitions, maps, plans, etc., in the place'; 'Stettin, 29 October 1806, at 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'seen and approved the present capitulation to be carried out. The Baron de Romberg, governor'; 'at the headquarters of Möhringen, 29 October 1806. The brigadier general, Lasalle'; as in claim side-a-command for Belliard's approval and the heading of his letter; 'I have the honour to report to you that the commandant of Stettin capitulated at 1 o'clock in the morning'; Murat, as in claim side-a-strength for the heading and the hussars at the gates; Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command for the night to the 30th and Lasalle's entry, and in claim side-a-strength for the march out; 'the Grand Duke of Berg reported to Napoleon at 5 o'clock in the morning: "Your Majesty's hussars will take possession of the gates of the town"'; Lasalle, as in claims side-b-strength-french for the heading and side-a-strength for the glacis; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor. Pasewalk, 31 October 1806'; 'the division of General Gazan with the brigade of General Claparède are at Stettin. After the enemy had capitulated, the rumour was spread that the Russians were coming, and part of the garrison had taken up its arms again. Everything has returned to order' (OCR).

claims.value: Höpfner: as all the Prussian cavalry had gone back through the fortress, there was no news at all of the enemy's approach. At midday on the 29th a cannon shot announced his arrival; the alarm was beaten and the garrison went to its posts, but only a few troops of cavalry were seen. The first parlementaire claimed that 100,000 men surrounded the fortress and that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau; the second, that Lasalle stood with the advance guard ½ mile away and that the corps of Murat and Lannes would take the fortress the next morning with 30 to 40,000 men. The garrison had no idea of the negotiation and fired on the enemy horsemen.

claims.value: Side A sought the fortress and the pursuit beyond it. On 28 October Murat wrote that Lasalle was marching on Löcknitz to cut off Blücher's retreat and that he himself would be on Stettin the next day; he sent Belliard to Stettin to summon the commandant. With the capitulation he ordered Lasalle to move rapidly on Damm, and wrote that Lannes would have Stettin occupied by a regiment of his corps and that the garrison would be sent by the Angermünde road to Berlin; in a postscript he would leave a whole division at Stettin to occupy Schwedt, Damm and Pölitz and furnish the escort for the garrison.
claims.rationale: Murat's letters of 28 and 30 October: the headings and the order to Lasalle from the page images, the rest of the letter of 30 October from the OCR of pp. 526-527. English renderings (ours): Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Prenzlow, 28 October 1806'; 'General Lasalle is marching on Löcknitz, where he will sleep this evening, to cut off General Blücher's retreat; General Milhaud is moving on Pasewalk; tomorrow I shall be on Stettin'; Belliard, as in claim side-a-command for his mission; Murat, as in claim side-a-strength for the heading of 30 October; 'I order General Lasalle to move rapidly on Damm and to try to sei-'; 'Marshal Lannes is going to have Stettin occupied by a regiment of his army corps' (OCR); 'I am going to have the garrison of Stettin directed by the Angermünde road on Berlin' (OCR); 'instead of leaving a brigade, I shall leave a whole division at Stettin; it will occupy Schwedt, Damm and Pölitz, and furnish the necessary escort for the garrison' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B prepared the fortress late: only on 17 October did the Ober-Kriegs-Kollegium order it made ready against a violent attack, and only on the 20th did the government call up carpenters and workers from the country; for want of time the defence was confined to the main rampart and Fort Preussen, and the outworks were abandoned as wholly decayed. The governor answered the first summons that he would defend the fortress to the utmost, but then drafted terms to hand it over the next morning with free withdrawal and all marks of honour; the capitulation's first article asked free exit with arms and baggage to West and North Prussia or Silesia, and its fifth at least 24 hours for the troops to settle their affairs.

claims.value: Side A attacked in the sense of summoning the fortress: Lasalle summoned the fort and town in Murat's name and repeated the summons after a refusal, and a second parlementaire threatened the town. Side B, having first refused, negotiated and capitulated; its garrison fired on horsemen who rode too close until the governor forbade it. Höpfner says the enemy could have taken the fortress only by a regular siege, for which he was in no way equipped.
claims.rationale: Both sides' accounts describe the French summoning the place with cavalry and side B capitulating. The phase is left unresolved: Murat had written that he would be on Stettin and sent Belliard to summon the commandant, but Lasalle had begun the summons before Belliard came (claim side-a-command), so the passages read do not settle whether the summons was Lasalle's own initiative or Murat's order. English renderings (ours): the capitulation, as in claim side-a-command for the preamble; Höpfner, as in claims side-a-command for the second parlementaire, side-b-command for the governor's answer and the firing, and fortification for the siege; Belliard, as in claim side-a-command for his mission; Murat, as in claim side-a-objectives for 28 October.

Höpfner: the defensive preparations were confined to the main rampart and Fort Preussen, the outworks being abandoned; yet on 29 October, by a reliable report, the fortress was fully secured against a coup de main, so that the enemy could have taken it only by a regular siege of three weeks, for which he was in no way equipped; 100 guns were already mounted on the ramparts and the chief points of defence. The 24th Bulletin called it a place in good condition, well armed and well palisaded; Belliard did not think it a good fortress.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the fortress's works were permanent and held by side B, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's and the Bulletin's assessments differ from Belliard's and are kept as given. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claim side-b-objectives for the works; 'nevertheless on 29 October the fortress was, according to a reliable report, fully secured against a coup de main, so that the enemy could have made himself master of it only after a three-week'; 'regular siege, for which, however, he was in no way equipped'; as in claim side-b-strength for the guns on the ramparts; the Bulletin, as in claim side-b-strength-french; Belliard, as in claims side-a-command for the heading and side-a-information for his assessment (OCR); the capitulation, as in claim side-a-command for the fort.

open_questions: Deferred: Murat's letter to Bernadotte of 29 October, printed in a footnote that begins on Foucart t. II, p. 523, outside the registered section, whose heading and text were read only in the OCR, with its report of men and guns taken at the gates of Stettin by Murat's aide de camp Beaumont; the engineer officer's report and the return of prisoners and magazines that Belliard promised; the Emperor's letters of 31 October to Murat and to Soult (pp. 556-557); the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests, and of Romberg's court martial. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: Lannes's garrison and guns found at Stettin (p. 598), the Emperor's figures in his letters of 31 October (p. 556), and the figures in Murat's footnote letter (p. 524).

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. The only figure is the 800 cavalry and 2 guns before which the garrison laid down its arms on the morning of the 30th (Höpfner; Bodart's 800 hussars), a count at the outcome rather than of the force that summoned the place; no headcount for Lasalle's brigade, or for Victor's infantry that came up afterwards, was read. A return of Lasalle's brigade or Murat's situation reports could settle it.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the garrison (100 officers and 5184 men, Höpfner; 5,300 with 100 officers, Bodart; 5,500 taken, Lasalle; 6,000, the Bulletin); the guns (187 serviceable and 94 for emergencies, Höpfner, and 281, Bodart; 120, Lasalle; 160, the Bulletin); the hour of the capitulation (dated 6 in the evening of the 29th and approved by Belliard that night; 1 in the morning, Belliard; carried out in the night to the 30th with Lasalle in the town at 6 in the morning before it was signed, Höpfner) and of Murat's report (2 in the morning in its dateline, 5 in the morning in Höpfner); Romberg's rank (Major General in Bodart, General-Lieutenant in Höpfner and lieutenant-général in the capitulation); 'without a stroke of the sword' (Bodart) against Belliard's few cannon shots.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 281 guns are Höpfner's 187 and 94 and his 5,300 with 100 officers is Höpfner's 100 officers and 5184 men rounded up, by our arithmetic); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Murat's letter with the capitulation, Belliard's and Lasalle's letters and the 24th Bulletin from the page images, Murat's further orders and Lannes's and Belliard's continuations from the OCR); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Stettin passage names no source beyond 'a reliable report' on the state of the works).
